body.hook: The dotted quarter followed by an eighth is one of the most common rhythms in band music: it's in "Jingle Bells," in marches and in anthems. Once you can count it, it's everywhere.

study.title: The Power of the Dot
study.question: How do dotted rhythms work?
study.passage:
Dot rule (written for this lesson): a dot adds half the value of the note.
Half note (2) + dot (1) = dotted half (3 beats): "1 2 3."
Quarter (1) + dot (½) = dotted quarter (1½ beats): "1 & 2" then the eighth on "&": counted "1 (&) (2) &."
Tie connection: a dotted quarter sounds the same as a quarter tied to an eighth.
Activities: 1. Subdivide: count 4/4 as "1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &" out loud. 2. Clap the dotted quarter + eighth pattern while counting the "&s." 3. Play on Concert B♭ at 72 BPM, then on a scale: dotted quarter + eighth on each note. 4. Find it: the opening of "Jingle Bells" chorus ("Jin-gle bells, jin-gle bells, jin-gle all the way": the word "all" is a dotted quarter followed by "the" as an eighth). 5. Dotted half notes in 3/4: one note fills a whole bar.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; Jingle Bells is in the public domain.

body.objective: Students will be able to play syncopated patterns.
successCriteria: I can count syncopated rhythms using subdivision

body.hook: Band music, especially jazz, pop arrangements and marches, often puts notes between the beats. Syncopation can sound tricky on the page, but with subdividing it clicks.

vocabulary.definition: Accents on off-beats or weak beats.

study.title: Between the Beats
study.question: How do I read and play syncopation?
study.passage:
Syncopation steps (written for this lesson):
1. Subdivide: count "1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &" and tap the foot on numbers only.
2. Eighth-quarter-eighth: notes on 1, "&" of 1 (held through 2), and "&" of 2. Count "1 & (2) &." Your foot taps on beat 2 while the note is held, not when a new note starts.
3. Tied syncopation: an eighth on "&" of 4 tied to the next bar's beat 1. The note starts early and holds over the bar line.
4. Practice line at 72 BPM: | ♩ ♪♩♪ ♩ | ♪♩♪ ♩ ♩ | on Concert B♭ then on scale notes.
5. Band application: find syncopations in the current concert piece; mark the counts in pencil above the notes.
6. Steady check: half the band plays steady quarters while the other half plays syncopation, then swap.

body.objective: Students will be able to read key signatures.
successCriteria: I can read key signatures for common band keys
I can name the order of flats and sharps
I can play concert B♭, E♭ and F scales with the correct notes
body.hook: Those sharps and flats at the start of every line aren't decoration. The key signature tells you which notes to change all the way through the piece, and forgetting it is the most common wrong-note mistake in band.

vocabulary.definition: Sharps or flats at the start of each line applying to the whole piece.
Lowers a note by a half step.
Raises a note by a half step.
A sharp, flat or natural added in the music, lasting until the end of the bar.
The key as it sounds for the whole band.

study.title: Reading the Key
study.question: How do key signatures tell me which notes to play?
study.passage:
Key signature guide (written for this lesson):
Order of flats: B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭ C♭ F♭ ("Battle Ends And Down Goes Charles's Father"). Order of sharps: F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯ E♯ B♯ (the reverse).
Common concert keys: Concert F: 1 flat (B♭); Concert B♭: 2 flats (B♭, E♭); Concert E♭: 3 flats (B♭, E♭, A♭).
Your part: transposing instruments see a different key signature. For Concert B♭: clarinet and trumpet (B♭ instruments) see C major (no sharps or flats); alto sax (E♭) sees G major (1 sharp, F♯); horn (F) sees F major (1 flat).
Accidentals: last only to the end of the bar; a natural cancels.
Activities: 1. Name the flats in each concert key. 2. Circle notes affected by the key signature in a practice line. 3. Play concert B♭, E♭ and F scales one octave, slowly. 4. Spot the accidental: in a line with an accidental, what happens in the next bar?
